description: Health monitoring is an important process wherever people are, either on earth or at space missions: so, by collecting and monitoring data during missions they may not know what does these values indicate or how they can react urgently to an emergency.
summary:
Vitanaut is an interactive health-management platform for astronauts on long-duration space missions. Crew members log daily habits such as exercise, sleep, nutrition, hydration and mental-health practices, while wearable data tracks heart rate, HRV, stress, sleep and activity. A guideline-based warning system compares readings with NASA-informed ranges and clearly labeled app thresholds, alerting astronauts when values leave healthy limits and explaining the consequences and immediate actions. An AI flight-health assistant helps users interpret symptoms, manage stress and add tailored habits to their routines.
Its distinguishing feature is an adaptive digital garden that visualizes health: stones represent muscle and bone health, flowers represent cardiovascular health, birds reflect psychological well-being, and trees show overall consistency. As routines improve, the garden evolves with the astronaut. By making health monitoring proactive, engaging and personalized, Vitanaut encourages astronauts to take an active role in protecting their health throughout a mission.
details:
Vitanaut brings six daily habit domains into one place: sleep, exercise, nutrition, hydration, mental health and symptom reporting. The crew member checks in briefly each day, wearable and cabin data fill in the rest, and the platform compares the result with a personal baseline and with thresholds taken from NASA sources. An assistant explains what changed and suggests one or two small adjustments, while a digital garden shows the crew member’s health as a living landscape.

Every rule in the platform is traceable. Each parameter carries a named source: a NASA standard, a NASA recommendation, NASA operational practice, a trend with no numeric limit, or an explicitly labelled app default. The platform never presents an app default as a NASA limit.

Astronauts on long missions live for months inside a few modules with the same small crew, far from family and familiar routines. The health effects are usually gradual rather than dramatic: sleep slips by an hour, exercise sessions are skipped, fluid intake falls, mood flattens. By the time a problem is obvious, performance and well-being may already be affected. Communication delays of up to about twenty minutes each way on a Mars mission make real-time ground monitoring impossible, so the crew needs a tool that helps them notice drift and act on it themselves.

The primary users are astronauts on the International Space Station, Artemis, Gateway and future Mars missions. Flight surgeons and mission planners are secondary users: they receive trends, adherence and flagged parameters rather than isolated readings. The same design can support analog crews, remote workers and patients managing long-term conditions on Earth. It matters because long-duration missions will not have a clinician watching every day in real time, and because prevention is cheaper and safer than treating a problem after it has developed.
